## Paper

## Abstract

Nature’s redox enzymes achieve remarkable selectivity by organizing active sites with precise spatial control, an ability difficult to replicate in synthetic systems. Inspired by this, we report a class of stable, metal-free bicarbenium-based molecular catalysts that undergo electrochemical two-electron reduction to form biradical intermediates. These biradicals are confined within a rigid xanthene bridge (~4.3 Å), creating a spatially defined pocket that engages paramagnetic substrates, such as O₂ and NO, resembling nature’s synergistic catalysis. This biradical-mediated synergistic catalysis enables highly selective two-electron oxygen reduction (99.3% H₂O₂ selectivity, 96.8% Faradaic efficiency, 2.21 mol g⁻¹ h⁻¹ productivity) and three-electron nitric oxide reduction (NH₂OH as major product, 87.2% Faradaic efficiency, 1.68 mol g⁻¹ h⁻¹ productivity). Experimental and computational studies confirm the sustained redox cycling, supported by favorable spin-pairing and substrate binding geometries, which enhance both catalytic selectivity and efficiency. This work presents a blueprint for pathway-specific, radical-mediated catalysis, offering new design principles for metal-free electrocatalytic platforms that exploit open-shell reactivity.

---

## Introduction

Nature has evolved remarkably efficient redox catalytic systems, where spatially organized active centers cooperatively mediate complex multi-electron transformations that are difficult to replicate synthetically1–3. For instance, cytochrome c oxidase (CcO) catalyzes the four-electron oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) in mitochondria via a binuclear metal center that stabilizes reactive intermediates (Fig. 1a)4. In contrast, NADPH oxidase selectively promotes the one-electron ORR to generate superoxide by integrating a flavin cofactor and two spatially separated metal sites to achieve selective oxygen activation (Fig. 1a)5. These biological systems exemplify how synergistic catalysis enables exceptional control over redox processes.

Despite efforts to emulate these biological principles, synthetic cooperative catalysts often suffer from limited structural precision, structural heterogeneity and poorly defined site distributions hinder the identification and isolation of the truly active motifs. Moreover, controlling the electronic and spatial interactions between adjacent sites is critically challenging, often leading to compromised selectivity and efficiency11–13. Molecular catalysts offer atomic-level tunability, enabling systematic reactivity modulation and precise mechanistic investigation14–16. While metal-centered designs remain dominant due to their redox versatility, they face issues such as stability, limited synthetic flexibility, and challenges in fine-tuning selectivity17–19. In this context, metal-free catalysts are emerging as promising alternatives, offering high structural tunability and potential for sustainable catalysis20–24.

Radicals play a central role in many biological and synthetic redox systems, enabling mechanistic pathways inaccessible to closed-shell species25–27. It has been demonstrated that triaryl carbon radicals can effectively activate O₂ via spin-pairing interactions, leveraging the biradical triplet nature of O₂ (Fig. 1b)28–32. Moreover, two such radicals can cooperatively bind O₂ to form a peroxide-linked intermediate. The inherent instability of such intermediate allows for multiple pathways, including reversion to O₂, generation of H₂O₂, or O-O bond cleavage under further reduction. These features make carbon-centered radicals particularly attractive for the activation and transformation of open-shell substrates.

A full catalytic cycle can be envisioned for triaryl carbon radicals in ORR (Fig. 1c, using ORR as the example hereafter): two radicals bind O₂ to form a peroxide intermediate (i), which undergoes stepwise protonation to release H₂O₂ and generate the carbenium (ii). Carbenium species can receive electrons to regenerate the active radicals, completing the cycle (iii). However, multiple degradation pathways, such as self-dimerization (iv), reductive protonation (v), unwanted side reaction and/or hydrolysis of intermediates (vi–vii)33,34, can compete, necessitating molecular designs that stabilize various intermediates to ensure selective and efficient turnover.

The binding geometry of O₂ at active sites further influences catalytic outcomes. Three conventional modes, Griffiths, Yeager, and Pauling types, govern selectivity and efficiency (Fig. 1d)35. Griffiths and Yeager involve side-on adsorption and tend to promote O-O bond cleavage, favoring the 4e- pathway, but often suffer from selectivity. Pauling-type end-on binding better preserves the O-O bond and thus supports the 2e- pathway, but it faces the issue of insufficient activation. Therefore, both active site architecture and electronic structure must be tailored to balance substrate binding, activation, and product selectivity.

Guided by principles of enzymatic dual-site synergy, carbenium/radical reactivity and substrate binding geometries, we designed a class of persistent bicarbenium scaffolds featuring a rigid xanthene bridge that positions the two carbenium centers ~4.3 Å apart (Fig. 1e). Upon electrochemical 2e- reduction, these scaffolds generate biradical intermediates that form a spatially confined pocket, ideally suited for engaging open-shell paramagnetic diatomic substrates such as O₂ and NO. These metal-free catalysts promote highly selective and efficient 2e- ORR (up to 99.3% selectivity, 96.8% Faradaic efficiency (FE) and 2.21 mol g⁻¹ h⁻¹ H₂O₂ productivity) and 3e- NORR (NH₂OH as major product with 87.2% FE and 1.68 mol g⁻¹ h⁻¹ productivity). This work demonstrates the power of biradical-mediated synergistic catalysis enabled by robust bicarbenium architecture and offers a general design strategy for next-generation, metal-free electrocatalysts, especially for redox transformations of open-shell substrates.

---

## Results

Synthesis and structural characterization
The dibromoxanthene bridge (1) was synthesized following reported procedures36. Three anthrone analogues (2–4), with heterocycles introduced to modulate electronic properties via inductive and resonance effects, thereby stabilizing both the carbenium and key catalytic intermediates, were prepared (Fig. 2a). Lithiation of 1, followed by nucleophilic addition to the anthrones, yielded dihydroxyl precursors (C-C-2OH, O-C-2OH, and S-C-2OH). The lower yield of S-C-2OH likely arises from sulfur’s more substantial electron-donating effect as well as more effective lone pair electron delocalization across the anthrone unit, which significantly reduces the electrophilicity of the carbonyl (resisting nucleophilic attack). The dihydroxyl precursors were dissolved in acetonitrile and treated with aqueous HBF₄ to afford the corresponding bicarbenium compounds via acid-mediated dehydration. The reaction progress was monitored by UV-vis spectroscopy, where characteristic absorption bands associated with carbenium species emerged and stabilized within 1 h (Supplementary Figs. 28–30)37–39. After solvent removal and recrystallization from diethyl ether, the bicarbenium compounds, C-C²⁺ (brownish yellow), O-C²⁺ (brownish red), and S-C²⁺ (brownish red), were isolated in nearly quantitative yields.

The chemical structures were confirmed by 1H, 13C, and 19F NMR spectroscopy, as well as high-resolution mass spectrometry (Supplementary Figs. 1–15 and 20–25). The single crystals of C-C²⁺ were obtained by slow evaporation from their acetonitrile solution, while single crystals of O-C²⁺ and S-C²⁺ were obtained via slow diffusion of diethyl ether into their acetonitrile solutions (Supplementary Figs. 60–62 and Supplementary Tables 8–10). X-ray crystallographic analysis revealed a cofacial spatial arrangement of the two carbenium centers in all three bicarbeniums (Fig. 2b). S-C²⁺ exhibits a more coplanar configuration due to additional sulfur-sulfur interactions. Intramolecular distances between the two carbenium centers were determined to be 4.61, 4.43, and 4.29 Å for C-C²⁺, O-C²⁺, and S-C²⁺, respectively, which are suitable for the activation of diatomic molecules. In the solid-state packing structures (Fig. 2c), the BF₄⁻ counter-ions are positioned in the intermolecular voids, leaving the bicarbenium sites sterically unencumbered and accessible for interaction with substrates. Notably, the arrangement of bicarbenium molecules indicates that each pair of intramolecular carbenium centers is well isolated from those neighboring molecules. This minimizes intermolecular interference between active sites and thus can effectively preserve the integrity of the intramolecular dual-site architecture and promotes synergistic catalysis at the molecular level.

These bicarbenium compounds show stable behavior under ambient conditions and in water, underscoring their suitability for catalytic applications in practical environments. To evaluate their robustness, a systematic pH-dependent stability study was conducted by adjusting the pH of their acetonitrile solutions using aqueous HCl or NaOH (Supplementary Figs. 31–33). The results revealed that C-C²⁺ remains stable only under acidic conditions (pH ≤ 6), while undergoing hydrolysis near neutral pH. In contrast, O-C²⁺ and S-C²⁺ displayed significantly enhanced tolerance, retaining structural integrity up to pH 9 and pH 12, respectively. The stability of these tertiary carbenium centers is initially supported by charge delocalization into adjacent aryl rings, while the use of O-xanthene and S-xanthene backbones provides additional stabilization via inductive donation effect and more effective charge delocalization through extended π-conjugation (Supplementary Fig. 65). In particular, sulfur, with its stronger electron-donating character and greater ability to engage in π-conjugation, confers higher stability to S-C²⁺.

Electronic and electrochemical properties
C-C²⁺, O-C²⁺, and S-C²⁺ exhibit intense absorption features in the UV-vis region (Fig. 3a). Specifically, C-C²⁺ displays a dominant absorption band with a maximum (λmax) at 407 nm, whereas O-C²⁺ and S-C²⁺ show two major absorption bands at 360/454 nm and 376/496 nm, respectively. The progressive red shift in absorption as well as emergence of new absorption band from C-C²⁺ to S-C²⁺ can be attributed to both a stronger inductive donation effect and enhanced π-conjugation within the xanthene-based carbenium, induced by O- and S-heterocycles. Based on their optical transitions, the optical band gaps of C-C²⁺, O-C²⁺, and S-C²⁺ were approximately 2.52, 1.83, and 1.72 eV, respectively. Cyclic voltammetry (CV) measurements in argon-saturated acetonitrile solution revealed that all three bicarbeniums exhibited two well-defined, reversible redox waves (Fig. 3b). When the first electron occupies the LUMO of the bicarbenium, it forms a radical cation, making subsequent reduction more difficult, thus the second redox wave appeared at lower potential. The first reduction onset potentials were measured at −0.05 V, −0.25 V, and −0.28 V (vs. Fc/Fc⁺) for C-C²⁺, O-C²⁺, and S-C²⁺, respectively, corresponding to the single-electron reduction from the bicarbenium (C⁺⁺C) state to the radical carbenium (C⁺•C) intermediate. The second reduction waves, observed at −0.22 V, −0.45 V, and −0.47 V, reflect the further one-electron reduction to the biradical (C••C) state. The stability of these diradical intermediates was monitored by ESR spectroscopy (Supplementary Figs. 108–110). The good reversibility of both redox steps underscores the high electrochemical stability of these molecular systems in all redox states. The frontier molecular orbital energy levels (HOMO and LUMO) were estimated to be −4.75/−2.50 eV for C-C²⁺, −4.55/−2.72 eV for O-C²⁺, and −4.52/−2.80 eV for S-C²⁺ (vs. vacuum, Fig. 3c). The rather low LUMO level of C-C²⁺ suggests a strong tendency to accept electrons, which may raise concerns of undesirable side reactions (like water oxidation reaction) under certain conditions40. This issue is addressed in detail in a later section.

In contrast, CV measurements in O₂-saturated acetonitrile revealed irreversible redox waves, suggesting that the reduced biradical intermediates readily react with O₂ (Supplementary Figs. 34–36). This observation supports the potential of these bicarbeniums to electrochemically activate molecular oxygen. To further investigate the reduction process and subsequent O₂ activation, chemical reduction using zinc powder was employed as a rapid electron source. The resulting biradical intermediates (C••C) were characterized by electron spin resonance (ESR) spectroscopy. ESR spectra of the reduced biradicals exhibited intense signals with g-values of 2.0028, 2.0031, and 2.0038 for C-C²⁺, O-C²⁺, and S-C²⁺, respectively (Fig. 3d, Supplementary Figs. 37 and 39). (Please also refer to the stepwise generation of mono-radical and diradical species via in situ ESR measurements, Supplementary Fig. 107) The higher g-values for S-C²⁺ suggest spin delocalization into the sulfur atoms, consistent with calculated spin density distributions (Supplementary Fig. 65). Variable-temperature (VT) ESR measurements from 273 to 153 K showed an increase in signal intensity with decreasing temperature (Fig. 3e), and the product of the ESR intensity (I) and temperature (T) remained nearly constant (Fig. 3f), suggesting negligible magnetic coupling between the two radical centers41. Similar observations were also found for C-C²⁺ and O-C²⁺ (Supplementary Figs. 38 and 40). This behavior is indicative of a singlet-triplet bistable state, in which the energy gap between spin states is minimal. Such spin flexibility is particularly advantageous for the activation of substrates with a triplet ground state.

Upon bubbling O₂ into the acetonitrile solution of the biradical intermediates, precipitates gradually formed, indicating the generation of COOC peroxide intermediates, which exhibit poor solubility in acetonitrile. These solids were collected by filtration and subsequently redissolved in deuterated DCM for further 1H NMR and mass spectrometry analysis. Taking S-COOC as an example, the 1H NMR spectrum appeared complex (Fig. 3h), likely due to multiple possible orientations of the peroxide bridge42 and concurrent reactions such as protonation and partial desorption (Supplementary Fig. 91). Despite the complexity, mass spectrometry provided clear evidence for the formation of the COOC peroxide intermediate (Fig. 3j). Besides, no obvious mass peaks corresponding to non-cooperative or single-site catalysis were detected in the higher mass range. To probe the catalytic cycle, excess aqueous HBF₄ as a proton source was added to the S-COOC solution, immediately restoring the characteristic dark red color of S-C²⁺. This regeneration was further confirmed by 1H NMR (Fig. 3g, i), indicating release of peroxide product and recovery of the bicarbenium. Similar catalytic cycling behavior was observed for O-C²⁺ (Supplementary Figs. 16, 17 and 26), whereas the higher relative mass spectrometric intensity of the peroxide-linked intermediate detected for S-C²⁺ highlights its enhanced capacity to stabilize this key species (Supplementary Figs. 26, 27). In contrast, isolation of the peroxide intermediate for C-C²⁺ proved difficult, likely due to its lower stabilization towards the intermediates.

Nevertheless, it offered a valuable opportunity to investigate the potential catalyst decomposition/competing pathways, given the low LUMO level of C-C²⁺ and its limited ability to stabilize reaction intermediates. To investigate this, two acetonitrile solutions of C-C²⁺ (each containing one drop of pH 7 pure water for accelerating side reactions) were prepared. One was stored under an argon (Ar) atmosphere, while the other was exposed to air. Both were left to evaporate slowly over several days (about 10 days for the Ar atmosphere sample and 3 days for the air-exposed sample). In the Ar-protected sample, the solution faded to pale yellow, while the air-exposed sample became colorless, both indicating decomposition of C-C²⁺. Single crystals were successfully isolated from both cases. X-ray crystallographic analysis revealed the formation of a protonated C-C-2H product under Ar, whereas the air-exposed sample yielded the corresponding hydroxyl precursor C-C-2OH (Supplementary Figs. 62, 63 and Tables 11, 12). These findings suggest the presence of a potential decomposition/competing pathway, although it occurs more slowly and at higher pH. Under inert conditions, C-C²⁺ underwent reductive protonation, with water acting as the electron donor and becoming oxidized. In the presence of O₂, the formation of a transient COOC peroxide intermediate likely underwent product desorption with water as both the electron and proton source. Once OH⁻ is accumulated, C-C²⁺ undergoes hydrolysis, resulting in the dihydroxyl precursor. The same trials for O-C²⁺ and S-C²⁺ reflected that their structures remained intact. Overall, these results revealed competing reductive protonation and hydrolysis pathways that may gradually deactivate the carbenium species for the case of C-C²⁺ due to a lack of additional stabilization as compared to O-C²⁺ and S-C²⁺.

Electrocatalysis
Having developed a comprehensive understanding of the molecular structures and redox properties of these bicarbenium compounds, we next evaluated their electrocatalytic performance toward the reduction of O₂ and NO. Catalyst inks of C-C²⁺, O-C²⁺, and S-C²⁺ were prepared by dispersing the compounds with carbon black and Nafion binder to enhance electrical conductivity and compatibility with aqueous electrolytes for heterogeneous electrocatalysis43.

ORR electrocatalysis. CV measurements were first conducted on a rotating disk electrode (RDE) in both Ar- and O₂-saturated 0.1 M HClO₄ (Supplementary Fig. 52). In Ar-saturated conditions, no apparent redox features were observed in the range of 0.2–1.0 V (vs. RHE). In contrast, well-defined cathodic waves appeared at ~0.4-0.7 V (vs. RHE) under O₂-saturation, highlighting the electrocatalytic activity of all three catalysts toward the ORR. To further assess their performance, linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) curves were recorded at varying rotation rates (400–2400 rpm) in O₂-saturated electrolyte (Supplementary Figs. 53–55). The increasing current density with higher rotation rates reflects improved mass transport through convective diffusion, supporting faster reaction kinetics. Their electrocatalytic properties were further probed using rotating ring-disk electrode (RRDE) measurements to determine the onset potentials, Tafel slopes, electron transfer numbers (n), and H₂O₂ selectivity at 1600 rpm and a scan rate of 10 mV s⁻¹ (Fig. 4a). The onset potentials for C-C²⁺, O-C²⁺ and S-C²⁺ were determined to be 0.665, 0.686, and 0.696 V (vs. RHE), respectively (defined as the potential at which the current density reaches 0.1 mA cm⁻²). The more positive onset potential or small overpotential for S-C²⁺ catalysts suggests that S-C²⁺ initiates ORR more readily. Tafel analysis revealed slopes of 63.7, 59.7, and 53.1 mV dec⁻¹ for C-C²⁺, O-C²⁺, and S-C²⁺, respectively (Fig. 4b), with the lower slope of S-C²⁺ indicating faster reaction kinetics. At 0.2 V (vs. RHE), the current densities reached approximately 1.77, 2.27, and 2.88 mA cm⁻², for C-C²⁺, O-C²⁺, and S-C²⁺, respectively, in line with their relative catalytic activities. The LSV comparison with commercial carbon black and Pt/C and the electrochemical surface area (ECSA) measurements revealed a 2e- reaction pathway feature for these bicarbenium catalysts and their intrinsic catalytic activity can be attributed to the bicarbenium sites (see Supplementary Figs. 105, 106). The electron transfer numbers (n) remained relatively constant between 0.2–0.6 V (vs. RHE, Fig. 4c), with values of 2.32, 2.12, and 2.03 for C-C²⁺, O-C²⁺, and S-C²⁺, respectively, suggesting that these catalysts predominantly follow a two-electron ORR pathway to produce H₂O₂. Correspondingly, the H₂O₂ selectivity across the same potential window was 93.2%, 96.8%, and 99.3%, respectively (Fig. 4c). These findings demonstrate that all three bicarbenium systems exhibit high selectivity toward the two-electron ORR pathway, with S-C²⁺ showing the highest catalytic activity and product selectivity, followed by O-C²⁺ and C-C²⁺.

An H-type cell was assembled to quantitatively evaluate the H₂O₂ production rate and the corresponding FE. H₂O₂ quantification was performed using the conventional Ce(SO₄)₂ titration method44, calibrated via UV-vis spectrophotometry (Supplementary Fig. 43). The electrocatalysis reaction was conducted over 6 h, with aliquots of the catholyte collected hourly for analysis. All three catalysts, C-C²⁺, O-C²⁺, and S-C²⁺ demonstrated continuous H₂O₂ generation, with total yields of 668.7 μmol, 762.4 μmol, and 1076.5 μmol, respectively, after 6 hours (Fig. 4d and Supplementary Figs. 44, 46). The corresponding H₂O₂ production rates (κ) and FE were calculated at each time point (Fig. 4e and Supplementary Figs. 47–49). Both parameters remained stable throughout the experiment, with production rates of 1.36, 1.56, and 2.21 mol g⁻¹ h⁻¹ and FEs of 92.6%, 94.0%, and 96.8% for C-C²⁺, O-C²⁺, and S-C²⁺, respectively. (Please also refer to the performance and discussion in flow cell using the best performed S-C2+ catalyst, Supplementary Fig. 111) The catalyst durability was investigated at 0.4 V vs. RHE by chronoamperometric method (Fig. 4f). While both O-C²⁺ and S-C²⁺ exhibited good stability, with only 5.1% and 1.5% loss of current density respectively, after 60,000 s of operation, the stability of C-C²⁺ raised some concerns. Its current density showed a noticeable decline in the early stage, followed by a slight decrease in the later stage. As identified in the previous section, the presence of a competing reaction (reductive protonation and hydrolysis) could be responsible for the observed loss in catalytic activity. Nevertheless, the hydrolyzed species may gradually revert to carbeniums in the acid media, thus the loss of current density becomes less significant in a later stage. These results highlight the effective electrocatalytic performance of the bicarbenium catalysts, with performance competitive to that of previously reported catalysts under similar electrocatalytic conditions (Supplementary Table 6).

NORR electrocatalysis. Nitric oxide (NO) features a doublet ground state with a single unpaired electron whose spin density is primarily on the nitrogen atom but also delocalized over oxygen (about 65% vs 35%)45. This electronic structure suggests that our catalysts may be well-suited for the nitric oxide reduction reaction (NORR). Given its high activity in oxygen reduction and enhanced ability to initiate reactions and stabilize key intermediates, S-C²⁺ was chosen for detailed investigation of NORR. LSV in Ar- and NO-saturated 0.1 M HClO₄ revealed a pronounced increase in both onset potential and current density in the presence of NO (Fig. 4g), indicating efficient NO electroreduction. To estimate the electron transfer number, LSV curves were compared with those obtained using a polycrystalline Pt electrode under identical conditions, where Pt is known to reduce NO selectively to N₂O via a one-electron pathway at 0.2 V vs. RHE46. The diffusion-limiting current density (jd) of Pt was measured at 1.64 mA cm⁻², consistent with literature values, while S-C²⁺ exhibited a significantly higher jd of 5.02 mA cm⁻². This ~3.06-fold increase suggests a 3e⁻ transfer pathway for our bicarbenium catalyst in NORR. (Please refer to the SI for the NORR performances of O-C2+ and C-C2+, Supplementary Fig. 93)

An H-type cell was assembled to identify the reduction products and quantify the reaction performance. Based on the inferred electron transfer number, the likely products were narrowed to hydroxylamine (NH₂OH/NH₃OH⁺) and ammonia (NH₃/NH₄⁺). NH₂OH was quantified using a colorimetric method involving 8-quinolinol oxidation to a strongly absorbing dimer at 705 nm, while NH₃ was quantified using Nessler’s reagent at 420 nm, both calibrated via UV–vis spectrophotometry (Supplementary Figs. 50, 51)47. For safety, the electrolysis was carried out over 3 h, with hourly aliquots collected for analysis. S-C²⁺ showed continuous NH₂OH production with a total yield of 206.2 μmol (Fig. 4h), a steady rate of 1.68 mol g⁻¹ h⁻¹, and a FE of 87.8% (Fig. 4i). These findings underscore the high selectivity and efficiency of such bicarbenium catalysts for NORR, showing competitive performance compared with previously reported catalysts under comparable conditions (Supplementary Table 7).

Compared with the monocation S-C⁺ catalyst (see detailed characterization data in Supplementary Figs. 94–100), which was prepared using the same synthetic strategy, the bicarbenium catalysts exhibited enhanced selectivity and catalytic performance due to the synergistic mechanism.

Mechanism study
ORR mechanism. Comprehensive in situ spectroscopy and density functional theory (DFT) calculations were conducted to elucidate the catalytic activity and selectivity of the bicarbenium catalysts. In situ attenuated total reflectance Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (ATR-IR) was employed to probe the reaction pathway, with spectra collected across a potential range of 1.0 to 0.2 V vs. RHE (Fig. 5a and Supplementary Figs. 41, 42). Corresponding vibrational assignments were guided by the literature precedents and computed IR spectra (Supplementary Figs. 70–81)24,29,48,49. Taking S-C²⁺ as a representative example (Fig. 5a), several characteristic peaks were identified (Supplementary Table 4): the peak at 917 cm⁻¹ corresponds to O-O symmetric stretch in the *C-OO-C* peroxide-linked intermediate; The band at 1334 cm⁻¹ appeared at low potential is assigned to the C-O-O⁻ anion stretch from *COO⁻ intermediate (to form the *COOH intermediate by protonation). Peaks at 1183 and 1210 cm⁻¹ are attributed to the C-O symmetric stretch in the *C-OO-C* peroxide linkage and the C–OOH asymmetric stretch in the protonated *COOH intermediate, respectively. Besides, the broad signal at 3533 cm⁻¹ corresponds to O-H stretching in the *COOH intermediate. These spectral signatures suggest an ORR pathway wherein O₂ is first captured and reduced to form a *C-OO-C* peroxide-linked intermediate, followed by stepwise protonation to yield the *COOH species and ultimately release H₂O₂.

To complement the spectroscopic insights, DFT calculations were performed to elucidate the proposed reaction mechanism (Fig. 5b). Starting from the bicarbenium precursor, electron transfer from the electrode generates the key biradical intermediate. Geometry optimizations of both singlet and triplet states reveal minor energy differences of −0.38, −0.41, and −1.04 kcal mol⁻¹ for C-C²⁺, O-C²⁺, and S-C²⁺, respectively, suggesting a singlet-triplet bistable state with a slightly thermodynamic preference for the triplet ground state (Supplementary Table 13). These biradicals are highly reactive toward triplet-state O₂ by spin-pairing interactions that facilitate its reduction. Calculations indicated that the synergistic binding of O₂ via two radical centers to form a peroxide-linked intermediate is energetically more favorable than their non-cooperative, single-site interactions (Supplementary Figs. 68, 69). The first protonation step occurs with near-equal preference at either terminal site due to the nearly symmetric structure. This generates the *COOH intermediate, which upon further protonation releases H₂O₂ and regenerates the bicarbenium species for the next catalytic cycle. Similar pathways were observed for O-C²⁺ and C-C²⁺, as supported by both in situ ATR-FTIR and DFT results (Supplementary Figs. 41, 42). Free energy profiles constructed for C-C²⁺, O-C²⁺, and S-C²⁺ (Fig. 5c) illustrate a common ORR mechanistic framework: the bicarbenium-to-biradical transformation is endothermic and identified as the rate-determining step (RDS), whereas all subsequent steps, including formation of the peroxide-linked intermediate, first protonation to the *OOH intermediate, and second protonation for H₂O₂ release and catalyst regeneration, are exothermic. The computed energy barriers for biradical formation are 6.0, 19.2, and 12.9 kcal mol⁻¹ for C-C²⁺, O-C²⁺, and S-C²⁺, respectively. Although C-C²⁺ features the lowest energy barrier, attributable to its exceptionally low LUMO level (Fig. 3c), its overall catalytic performance is compromised by a competing reductive protonation pathway, as revealed by the corresponding energy profile (Supplementary Figs. 67, 112). A more systematic comparison provided by our microkinetic analysis (Supplementary Note 18) further demonstrates that, when both activation and quenching channels are considered, the apparent catalytic activity follows the experimental order of C-C²⁺ < O-C²⁺ < S-C²⁺.

NORR mechanism. Building on the mechanistic understanding established for the ORR catalysis, similar in situ spectroscopic and computational approaches were employed to elucidate the NORR pathway using the most promising S-C²⁺ catalyst. Specifically, in situ ATR-IR spectroscopy was conducted over a potential range of 0.3 to −0.2 V vs. RHE (Fig. 5d), revealing distinct vibrational features associated with various reaction intermediates. These spectral features were interpreted with the aid of computed IR spectra and referenced vibrational assignments (Supplementary Fig. 82-90)46,47,50. Several key bands were identified, supporting the stepwise transformation of NO during the catalytic cycle. The N•-O stretch at 1357 cm⁻¹ corresponds to the formation of a *C-N•O-C* nitroxide-linked intermediate. The subsequent protonation steps were evidenced by peaks at 1042 and 1122 cm⁻¹, attributed to the C-NHO-C asymmetric stretch in the monoprotonated *C-NHO-C* species and the C-NHOH stretch in the diprotonated *C-NHOH* intermediate, respectively. Additionally, a band at 1583 cm⁻¹, which emerged at more negative potentials, could be assigned to the C-NH-O⁻ anion stretch in the *C-NH-O⁻* intermediate (to form the *C-NH-OH* intermediate by protonation). The bands at 1206 and 1264 cm⁻¹, increasing in intensity from 0.1 V vs. RHE, are attributed to C-O and C-N stretches in various intermediates. Lastly, the broad absorption around 3560 cm⁻¹ is characteristic of O-H and N-H stretching modes in protonated species such as *C-NHO-C* and *C-NHOH*. These findings strongly suggest a reaction pathway in which NO is first captured via a reduction step to form the nitroxide intermediate, followed by sequential protonation leading to the release of NH₂OH.

DFT calculations were also performed to gain deeper insight into the proposed NORR mechanism catalyzed by S-C²⁺ (Fig. 5e). Similar to the ORR pathway, the reaction initiates with electron transfer from the electrode to the bicarbenium precursor, generating a biradical intermediate. This biradical, with high reactivity toward triplet-like NO, facilitates its reduction to form a C-N•O-C nitroxide intermediate. Spin density analysis indicated a delocalized unpaired electron, mostly residing on nitrogen, mirroring the electronic structure of free NO molecule (Supplementary Fig. 66). Therefore, the following protonation step is more favorable at the nitrogen atom, forming the monoprotonated *C-NHO-C* intermediate. The second protonation is energetically preferred at the oxygen atom, yielding the C-NHOH species. The final protonation releases NH₂OH and regenerates the original bicarbenium scaffold, completing the catalytic cycle (across S-C²⁺, O-C²⁺, and C-C²⁺, transition-state analyses show that C–O cleavage to form NH₂OH is kinetically favoured over N–O cleavage to form NH₃, explaining the high NH₂OH selectivity (87.8% FE) and only trace NH₃ observed experimentally, as summarized in Supplementary Figs. 113-114). The constructed free energy profile (Fig. 5f, the calculations were also performed for C-C²⁺ and O-C²⁺ for comparison) revealed that both the bicarbenium-to-biradical transition and the biradical-to-nitroxide linkage formation are endothermic. In contrast, all subsequent protonation steps are exothermic, facilitating smooth progression toward product formation and catalyst regeneration. The results reaffirm that the bicarbenium-to-biradical transition is the RDS, similar to the ORR process, with an energy barrier of 12.9 kcal mol⁻¹. However, the formation of the C-N•O-C nitroxide intermediate also presents a comparable barrier of 10.9 kcal mol⁻¹, giving rise to the relatively lower catalytic efficiency of NORR compared to ORR. The discrepancy can be attributed to the intrinsic doublet electronic structure of the NO molecule. Although its unpaired electron can delocalize between the N and O atoms, giving it a semblance of triplet character, it is inherently less compatible than triplet O₂ in engaging with the biradical intermediate. This diminished spin compatibility weakens the spin-pairing interactions, which likely contributes to the lower catalytic efficiency observed in NORR. Nevertheless, S-C²⁺ still exhibited good NORR performance, achieving high efficiency and selectivity despite the additional energetic demand. We also carried out the same microkinetic analysis for the NORR pathway (Supplementary Note 18), and the apparent activity trend remains C–C²⁺ < O–C²⁺ < S–C²⁺. Supplementary Videos 1 and 2 are provided to visualize the proposed ORR and NORR processes.

Electrocatalysis for closed-shell substrates. Beyond ORR and NORR, the electrocatalytic potential of S-C²⁺ was further explored with a range of commonly studied yet more inert closed-shell molecules. LSV measurements were conducted for the electrochemical reduction of N₂, CO₂, NO₂⁻, and NO₃⁻ (Supplementary Figs. 56–58). In each case, S-C²⁺ exhibited decreased onset potentials and elevated current densities, indicative of its ability to activate these closed-shell strongly bonded molecules51–53, likely facilitated by the interactions between the radical intermediates and the vacant orbitals of those molecules. The observed variations in activity likely stem from differences in molecular size and intrinsic electronic structure. While these preliminary results highlight the broader catalytic potential of bicarbenium systems, further studies are warranted to elucidate the underlying activation pathways and identify the resulting products.

## Methods

General methods
All reagents and starting materials were obtained from commercial suppliers and used without further purification, unless otherwise noted. Anhydrous THF was distilled from sodium-benzophenone solution immediately prior to use. Column chromatography was performed on silica gel 60 (Merck 40–60 nm, 230–400 mesh). The 1H, 13C and 19F NMR spectra were recorded in solution of CDCl₃/CD₃CN on Bruker DPX400 or DPX500 NMR spectrometers. All chemical shifts are quoted in ppm, relative to tetramethylsilane (TMS) with the residual solvent peak as a reference standard. High resolution mass spectrometry (MS) measurements were performed on a Finnigan TSQ7000 triple stage quadrupole mass spectrometer by atmospheric pressure chemical ionization (APCI) or on a Bruker MALDI-TOF Autoflex. UV-vis-NIR absorption spectra were recorded on a Shimadzu UV-3600 spectrophotometer. Electrochemical measurements were conducted using an Autolab PGSTAT302N workstation.

Synthesis of bicarbenium catalysts
The respective dihydroxyl precursors (50 mg), C-C-2OH, O-C-2OH or S-C-2OH, were dissolved in acetonitrile (5 ml) under argon. Tetrafluoroboric acid solution (48 wt% in H₂O, 0.5 ml) was slowly added and the suspension immediately turned into a dark color solution. After stirring for 2 h, the solvent was removed under reduced pressure. The crude product was recrystallized from diethyl ether, filtered and dried under reduced pressure to afford the bicarbenium compounds: C-C²⁺ (brownish yellow), O-C²⁺ (brownish red) and S-C²⁺ (brownish red), all in nearly quantitative yield. The more detailed synthesis and characterization data are included in Supplementary Information.

X-ray crystallography
The single crystals of C-C²⁺ were obtained by slow evaporation from its acetonitrile solution, while single crystals of O-C²⁺ and S-C²⁺ were obtained via slow diffusion of diethyl ether into their acetonitrile solutions. The single crystals of C-C-2H and C-C-2OH were obtained by slow evaporation from acetonitrile solutions of C-C²⁺ with 1 drop of pH 7 water in argon atmosphere and air-exposed condition, respectively, after several days (about 10 days for the Ar atmosphere sample and 3 days for the air-exposed sample). Crystallographic data have been deposited with the Cambridge Crystallographic Data Centre as supplementary publication no. CCDC 2448050 for C-C2+, 2448051 for O-C2+, 2448052 for S-C2+, 2448053 for C-C-2H and 2448055 for C-C-2OH. The X-ray intensity data were measured at low temperature (T=100 K), using a four circles goniometer Kappa geometry, Bruker AXS D8 Venture, equipped with an APEX-II detector. Frames were integrated with the Bruker SAINT software package. Data were corrected for absorption effects using the multi-scan method (SADABS)54. Molecule was solved with the software SHELXT55, using a Dual Space method. Refinement of the structure was performed by least squares procedures on weighted F² values using the SHELXL-version 2014/6 module56 in olex257.

ESR and VT-ESR
ESR spectra were recorded using a JEOL FA200 spectrometer operating at X-band frequency (~9.4 GHz). The respective samples were packed into quartz ESR tubes under an inert atmosphere. VT-ESR measurements were conducted from 273 K to 153 K with 10 K intervals, controlled by a variable temperature liquid nitrogen cryostat. Instrument parameters, including microwave power, modulation amplitude, and scan width, were carefully optimized for each sample to ensure accurate signal detection without saturation. Spectra were calibrated against an internal standard for g-factor determination.

Electrochemistry
Cyclic voltammetry (CV) measurements were performed in acetonitrile with a three-electrode cell, using 0.1 M tetrabutylammonium hexafluorophosphate (nBu₄NPF₆) as supporting electrolyte, Ag/AgCl as reference electrode, gold disk as working electrode, Pt wire as counter electrode, with a scan rate of 50 mV s⁻¹. The gold disk electrode was cleaned and polished with Al₂O₃ powders prior to use.

ORR electrocatalytic tests: The catalytic activity of catalysts was measured in 0.1 M HClO₄ electrolyte solution (pH=1). An ink of the respective catalyst was prepared by mixing 1.7 mg of catalyst and 1.3 mg carbon black with 250 μL of a 0.5 wt% Nafion solution (4/1 volume ratio between ethanol and 0.1 M HBF₄ water solution for stabilization), and further placed in an ultrasonic bath for 1 h. 12 μL of the solution was loaded onto the electrode and dried in air. The RRDE measurements were performed in a three-electrode, one-compartment cell at room temperature (25°C), equipped with a Pt wire counter electrode and an Ag/AgCl reference electrode. O₂ gas was purged into the 0.1 M HClO₄ electrolyte solution for 30 min. Linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) was performed in O₂-saturated 0.1 M HClO₄ electrolyte at an electrode rotation rate of 1600 rpm and a scan rate of 10 mV s⁻¹, with a ring potential held at +1.4 V vs. RHE. All potential scales were converted to RHE using:

E_RHE = E_Ag/AgCl + 0.059 × pH + 0.197 (1)

The H₂O₂ selectivity and electron transfer number were calculated using the following equations based on LSV curves:

H₂O₂ (%) = I_r / N / (I_d / N + I_r / N) × 2 × 100 (2)

n = 4 × I_d / (I_d + I_r / N) (3)

where I_r is the ring current, I_d is the disk current and N is the collection efficiency (0.29 after calibration).

The H₂O₂ production process was monitored using a self-assembled H-type cell with a three-electrode system with 0.1 M HClO₄ solution as both the catholyte and anolyte, which were separated by a Nafion 115 membrane (1.5 × 1.5 cm² DuPont). A carbon paper (1 × 1 cm²) with a microporous layer, spayed-coated with catalyst ink, was used as the working electrode. An Ag/AgCl and a carbon rod were applied as reference and counter electrode, respectively. The reaction was monitored under potentiostatic mode at 0.4 V vs. RHE for a consecutive 6 hours, with aliquots of the catholyte collected hourly for analysis. H₂O₂ quantification was performed using the conventional Ce(SO₄)₂ titration method, calibrated via UV–vis spectrophotometry. The production rate and FE for H₂O₂ generation were calculated based on:

rate: mol g_cat⁻¹ h⁻¹ = n_H2O2 / (L × t) (4)

FE (%) = 2 × n_H2O2 × F / Q × 100 (5)

where n_H2O2 is the quantity of H₂O₂ generated (mol), L is the catalyst loading (g), t is the duration (h), F is the Faraday constant, and Q is the total charge amount (C) derived from the current-time curve.

NORR electrocatalytic tests: the characterization of NORR followed similar procedures to ORR with some modifications. The electron transfer number was estimated by comparing the LSV current density of a polycrystalline Pt electrode at about 0.2 V vs. RHE with the current density of catalyst electrode at about −0.2 V vs. RHE under same conditions (0.1 M HClO₄ electrolyte and pH=1, 1600 rpm, and 10 mV s⁻¹). NH₂OH was quantified using a colorimetric method involving 8-quinolinol oxidation to a strongly absorbing dimer at 705 nm, while NH₃ was quantified using Nessler’s reagent at 420 nm, both calibrated via UV–vis spectrophotometry. For safety reasons, the electrolysis was carried out over 3 h, with hourly aliquots collected for analysis.

All reported potential and voltage values were iR-compensated (85%) using the automatic iR compensation function of the Autolab (Metrohm) electrochemical workstation with NOVA software.

In situ ATR-IR measurements
In situ attenuated total reflection Fourier transform infrared (ATR-IR) spectroscopy was conducted using a Nicolet iS50 FTIR spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific). A silicon prism coated with a thin gold film and the catalyst ink served as the working electrode, with a platinum mesh as the counter electrode and an Ag/AgCl electrode as the reference. Measurements were carried out in 0.1 M HClO₄ electrolyte. Prior to data acquisition, the electrolyte was saturated with high-purity O₂ (99.995%) by bubbling for 30 min. Spectra were recorded over a potential range of 0.2 to 1.0 V vs. RHE. Similar procedures were employed for nitric oxide (NO, 99.9%), with spectra collected over a potential window of −0.2 to 0.3 V vs. RHE.

Computational details
All density functional theory (DFT) calculations were carried out using the Gaussian 16 software58 package at the ωB97XD59/6–31G(d,p)60,61 level of theory. Solvent effects were incorporated using the SMD implicit solvation model with water as the solvent62. Electrostatic potential (ESP) maps and spin density were analyzed using Multiwfn version 3.863–65.

The Gibbs free energies of all reactants and intermediates are calculated by the equation:

G = E_elec + G_corr + RT ln(C_aq / C_gas) (6)

Where E_elec is the electronic energy of the species obtained from the self-consistent field (SCF) calculation, and G_corr represents the thermal correction derived from frequency analysis, which includes the zero-point energy (ZPE) as well as thermal contributions to enthalpy and entropy. The final term, RT ln(C_aq / C_gas), accounts for the standard-state conversion from the gas-phase reference state (1 atm) to the aqueous-phase reference state (1 mol L⁻¹), contributing an additional +1.89 kcal/mol.

The Gibbs free energy of the solvated proton (H⁺) in aqueous phase was taken as −270.29 kcal/mol. This value was obtained from the following equation:

G_H+ = G_gas_H+ + G_solv_H+ + RT ln(C_aq / C_gas) (7)

Where G_gas_H+ is the gas-phase Gibbs free energy of the proton (−6.28 kcal/mol)66, G_solv_H+ is the solvation free energy (−265.9 kcal/mol)67, and the standard state correction term RT ln(C_aq / C_gas) accounts for the transition from the gas-phase standard state (1 atm) to the aqueous-phase standard state (1 mol/L), which contributes +1.89 kcal/mol.

The Gibbs free energy of a free electron referenced to the reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) was calculated based on the RHE work function, using the relation:

E_RHE = E_SHE + 0.059 × pH (8)

The absolute potential of the standard hydrogen electrode (SHE) was taken as 4.44 eV68. At pH=1, this yields an RHE-referenced electron energy of 4.499 eV. Since electrons contribute to the Gibbs free energy as negative chemical potentials, this corresponds to −103.75 kcal/mol, calculated using the relation μ_e = −e × Φ, with 1 eV ≈ 23.06 kcal/mol.

Data availability
All data supporting the findings of this study are provided in the article and its Supplementary Information. Crystallographic data for the structures reported in this article have been deposited in the Cambridge Crystallographic Data Centre, under deposition numbers CCDC 2448050, 2448051, 2448052, 2448053 and 2448055. Copies of the data can be obtained free of charge via https://www.ccdc.cam.ac.uk/structures/. The authors declare that the data supporting the findings of this study are available within the paper, the source data and Supplementary Information files. Source data are provided with this paper.

### Reviewer 2

This study synthesized three well-defined metal-free molecular catalysts, among which S-C2+ exhibited excellent performance in both two-electron oxygen reduction and three-electron nitric oxide reduction. Interestingly, the authors proposed a biradical-mediated reaction mechanism. However, the confirmation of this mechanism lacks sufficient experimental evidence (see Q14). Additionally, the electrochemical performance of the catalyst was primarily evaluated in an H-cell (or RDEs), and data on its application in membrane electrode assemblies (MEAs) or flow cells are still lacking, limiting the impact of this research. Furthermore, while the authors synthesized three molecular catalysts, the differences in their electrochemical behavior were explained solely by the electronic effect on reaction energy barriers, which appears oversimplified. If the novelty of this work mainly stems from the biradical-mediated reaction mechanism, the inclusion of O-C2+ and C-C2+ may not be strictly necessary.
My specific comments are listed as follows:
1. The electronic structure depiction of the trityl radical in Figure 1b is incorrect. It is erroneously shown as having two electrons with parallel spins in two orbitals. This figure requires revision.
2. In the Supporting Information (SI), there is a lack of detailed explanations and descriptions for the spectra in Supplementary Figs. 1–26. The authors should provide a thorough analysis of each peak signal to allow readers to better understand the structural details of the synthesized molecules. Given that the successful synthesis of these molecular catalysts is a major innovation of this work, such comprehensive explanation is essential.
3. The mass spectrometry data provided by the authors should include a broader *m/z* range to allow readers to better assess the purity of the synthesized molecules. The authors do not appear to report the purity levels of the three catalysts. Although single-crystal structures of the corresponding molecules were obtained, the experimental section does not explicitly state whether the single-crystal samples were directly used for electrochemical testing. If not, the samples employed in the electrochemical measurements may contain impurities. The nature and concentration of such impurities should be reported, as this information is critical for evaluating whether the observed electrochemical behavior is influenced by these impurities.
4. In Supplementary Figs. 31-33, the authors investigated the structural stability of the molecular catalysts using UV-Vis spectroscopy, which is clearly insufficient. While changes in UV-Vis spectra can indicate structural instability, demonstrating molecular stability requires additional structural characterization data, such as mass spectrometry (MS) or nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy.
5. In Fig. 3a, the UV-Vis spectra of O-C and S-C exhibit two distinct peaks, while C-C shows only one. The authors should provide a clear explanation for this observed difference.
6. The assignment of the (C+/+C) state to (C+/*C) and subsequently to (C*/*C) in the CV (Fig. 3b) requires experimental validation. Structurally, the two C+ moieties exhibit symmetry—why then do they display distinct redox potentials? The authors must provide a convincing rationale for this observation. One feasible approach would involve monitoring EPR signals at varying potentials: if their assignment is correct, distinct radical species should be detectable at different applied potentials. Given that this work proposes a radical-involved electrocatalytic mechanism, the generation and evolution of radical intermediates are critical aspects that demand rigorous experimental proof.
7. If radicals truly participate in the ORR process, the reaction onset potential should closely align with either the first or second radical formation potential. However, the polarization curves reveal that the ORR onset potential lags behind the second CV peak by at least 0.3-0.4 V (Supplementary Figs. 34-36), which appears inconsistent with the proposed reaction pathway. Another intriguing observation is that under O₂ atmosphere, the higher-potential redox signal (first peak) nearly disappears, while the lower-potential redox peak remains largely intact. A deeper analysis of this phenomenon could provide valuable mechanistic insights. Additionally, the ORR polarization curves lack a critical reference dataset (e.g., Pt/C) for performance benchmarking, which is essential for evaluating the catalysts' practical relevance.
8. The authors assign the ESR signal at g = 2 to a C*-*C radical. However, the spectra lack hyperfine splitting. Carbon-centered radicals typically exhibit hyperfine coupling to nearby 1H nuclei. Furthermore, the schematic suggests conjugation with phenyl rings, where delocalization could also cause splitting. Why is the observed ESR signal a singlet rather than showing splitting? A convincing explanation for this apparent lack of hyperfine structure is required.
9. In Figs. 3g-3i, the authors present NMR spectra of the initial sample, the sample after O₂ purging, and the sample after HBF₄ treatment. However, prior to O₂ exposure, the system should also include the state after Zn powder addition. Shouldn't the corresponding NMR spectrum for this intermediate state be provided as well?
10. If the ESR measurement was performed ex situ? If a radical trapping agent (e.g., a spin trap) applied to stabilize and detect this radical signal? if no trap was used, data showing the stability of this radical ESR signal intensity over time are crucial to verify its stability during the measurement window and any subsequent experiments (e.g., variable-temperature ESR), ruling out signal changes due to radical decay.
11. There appears to be a contradiction between two key experimental observations: (1) C-C exhibits the highest radical formation potential (Fig. 3b), yet (2) demonstrates the lowest ORR activity (Fig. 4a). This inverse relationship challenges the proposed radical-driven mechanism. While the authors attempt to explain this discrepancy through computational studies (suggesting competitive hydrogenation pathways for C-C), such interpretation lacks robust experimental validation.
12. The assignment of the peak at ~917 cm⁻¹ in the in-situ ATR-IR spectra to the O-O stretching vibration requires stronger validation. The peak is weak, and its origin cannot be definitively distinguished from potential reduction features of the molecular catalyst itself at low potentials. Performing a control in situ ATR-IR experiment under an inert Ar atmosphere (non-reactive conditions) is necessary. Additionally, conducting an experiment using ¹⁸O₂ isotope labeling would provide much more compelling evidence for the assignment and the reaction mechanism. If correctly assigned to O-O, the vibrational peak should exhibit a predictable isotopic shift.
13. Post-reaction structural characterization of the catalysts should be rigorously performed, as radical-mediated processes may induce catalyst degradation.
14. The core mechanistic claim—that confined radicals within the rigid xanthene bridge facilitate O₂/NO reduction—requires rigorous validation of two critical aspects: (1) electrochemical generation of C*-*C radicals, and (2) formation of C-O-O-C intermediates. While the observed EPR signal (g=2.00338) after Zn reduction suggests radical formation, this non-electrochemical approach cannot confirm operational relevance; in-situ EPR measurements under applied potentials (without reactants) are essential to establish the potential-dependent radical generation. For the proposed C-O-O-C intermediate, the current FTIR evidence remains inconclusive due to the absence of isotopic labeling (e.g., ¹⁸O₂) experiments and background spectra for definitive peak assignment.

### Reviewer 3

In the manuscript titled "Biradical-mediated synergistic electrocatalysis using metal-free redox molecular catalysts," the authors report a class of metal-free bicarbenium-based molecular catalysts that undergo electrochemical two-electron reduction to form biradical intermediates, enabling highly selective oxygen and nitric oxide reduction to H2O2 and NH2OH, respectively. The authors combine synthesis, spectroscopy, electrocatalysis, and DFT calculations to explain the role of spatially confined biradicals in promoting cooperative substrate activation.
First of all, my expertise is in computational/theoretical chemistry, and I understand that I was invited to review this aspect. Regarding the computational (DFT) parts of this manuscript, I have several critical concerns, outlined below:
1. Although the DFT-computed reaction energy profiles show that the C-C2+ shows the minimal overpotential, while the O-C2+ shows the largest value, the experimental ORR trend (shown in Fig. 4a) follows the order of C-C2+ < O-C2+ < S-C2+. This discrepancy implies the possibility that the reaction path that the authors investigated is not responsible for the actual experimental situations. A direct comparison between the computed reaction energy profiles and experimental results is required.
2. While the DFT pathway toward NH2OH is proposed, the manuscript does not address whether continued protonation to NH3 is kinetically or thermodynamically less favorable. Since this is central to understanding the observed selectivity (87.8% FE to NH2OH), the authors should clarify whether NH3 formation was computationally examined or ruled out based on energetics.
3. The computational methods are not described with sufficient detail. Most critically, the manuscript lacks an information about the treatment of entropy and/or zero-point energy (ZPE). The authors should describe how the ZPE and thermal corrections were evaluated to compute the free energy quantities.
4. DFT often fails to accurately describe the spin states and related energetics of open-shell species. Some benchmarking of the chosen functional, especially for spin-sensitive energetics, is necessary to ensure reliability.
5. (General comment) The reaction energetics support the mechanistic proposal qualitatively, but the analysis lacks depth expected for a high-impact submission. The current DFT analysis remains largely descriptive.
In summary, this work presents an exciting new direction for metal-free electrocatalysis using biradical intermediates. The DFT results are encouraging and generally align with the experimental observations. However, to match the rigor of the synthetic and spectroscopic work, the computational section requires clarification, benchmarking, and deeper mechanistic analysis.

## Paper

## Abstract

Nature’s redox enzymes achieve remarkable selectivity by organizing active sites with precise spatial control, an ability difficult to replicate in synthetic systems. Inspired by this, we report a class of stable, metal-free bicarbenium-based molecular catalysts that undergo electrochemical two-electron reduction to form biradical intermediates. These biradicals are confined within a rigid xanthene bridge (~4.3 Å), creating a spatially defined pocket that engages paramagnetic substrates, such as O₂ and NO, resembling nature’s synergistic catalysis. This biradical-mediated synergistic catalysis enables highly selective two-electron oxygen reduction (99.3% H₂O₂ selectivity, 96.8% Faradaic efficiency, 2.21 mol g⁻¹ h⁻¹ productivity) and three-electron nitric oxide reduction (NH₂OH as major product, 87.2% Faradaic efficiency, 1.68 mol g⁻¹ h⁻¹ productivity). Experimental and computational studies confirm the sustained redox cycling, supported by favorable spin-pairing and substrate binding geometries, which enhance both catalytic selectivity and efficiency. This work presents a blueprint for pathway-specific, radical-mediated catalysis, offering new design principles for metal-free electrocatalytic platforms that exploit open-shell reactivity.

## Introduction

Nature has evolved remarkably efficient redox catalytic systems, where spatially organized active centers cooperatively mediate complex multi-electron transformations that are difficult to replicate synthetically1–3. For instance, cytochrome c oxidase (CcO) catalyzes the four-electron oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) in mitochondria via a binuclear metal center that stabilizes reactive intermediates (Fig. 1a)4. In contrast, NADPH oxidase selectively promotes the one-electron ORR to generate superoxide by integrating a flavin cofactor and two spatially separated metal sites to achieve selective oxygen activation (Fig. 1a)5. These biological systems exemplify how synergistic catalysis enables exceptional control over redox processes.

Despite efforts to emulate these biological principles, synthetic cooperative catalysts often suffer from limited structural precision, structural heterogeneity and poorly defined site distributions hinder the identification and isolation of the truly active motifs. Moreover, controlling the electronic and spatial interactions between adjacent sites is critically challenging, often leading to compromised selectivity and efficiency11–13. Molecular catalysts offer atomic-level tunability, enabling systematic reactivity modulation and precise mechanistic investigation14–16. While metal-centered designs remain dominant due to their redox versatility, they face issues such as stability, limited synthetic flexibility, and challenges in fine-tuning selectivity17–19. In this context, metal-free catalysts are emerging as promising alternatives, offering high structural tunability and potential for sustainable catalysis20–24.

Radicals play a central role in many biological and synthetic redox systems, enabling mechanistic pathways inaccessible to closed-shell species25–27. It has been demonstrated that triaryl carbon radicals can effectively activate O₂ via spin-pairing interactions, leveraging the biradical triplet nature of O₂ (Fig. 1b)28–32. Moreover, two such radicals can cooperatively bind O₂ to form a peroxide-linked intermediate. The inherent instability of such intermediate allows for multiple pathways, including reversion to O₂, generation of H₂O₂, or O-O bond cleavage under further reduction. These features make carbon-centered radicals particularly attractive for the activation and transformation of open-shell substrates.

A full catalytic cycle can be envisioned for triaryl carbon radicals in ORR (Fig. 1c, using ORR as the example hereafter): two radicals bind O₂ to form a peroxide intermediate (i), which undergoes stepwise protonation to release H₂O₂ and generate the carbenium (ii). Carbenium species can receive electrons to regenerate the active radicals, completing the cycle (iii). However, multiple degradation pathways, such as self-dimerization (iv), reductive protonation (v), unwanted side reaction and/or hydrolysis of intermediates (vi–vii)33,34, can compete, necessitating molecular designs that stabilize various intermediates to ensure selective and efficient turnover.

The binding geometry of O₂ at active sites further influences catalytic outcomes. Three conventional modes, Griffiths, Yeager, and Pauling types, govern selectivity and efficiency (Fig. 1d)35. Griffiths and Yeager involve side-on adsorption and tend to promote O-O bond cleavage, favoring the 4e- pathway, but often suffer from selectivity. Pauling-type end-on binding better preserves the O-O bond and thus supports the 2e- pathway, but it faces the issue of insufficient activation. Therefore, both active site architecture and electronic structure must be tailored to balance substrate binding, activation, and product selectivity.

Guided by principles of enzymatic dual-site synergy, carbenium/radical reactivity and substrate binding geometries, we designed a class of persistent bicarbenium scaffolds featuring a rigid xanthene bridge that positions the two carbenium centers ~4.3 Å apart (Fig. 1e). Upon electrochemical 2e- reduction, these scaffolds generate biradical intermediates that form a spatially confined pocket, ideally suited for engaging open-shell paramagnetic diatomic substrates such as O₂ and NO. These metal-free catalysts promote highly selective and efficient 2e- ORR (up to 99.3% selectivity, 96.8% Faradaic efficiency (FE) and 2.21 mol g⁻¹ h⁻¹ H₂O₂ productivity) and 3e- NORR (NH₂OH as major product with 87.2% FE and 1.68 mol g⁻¹ h⁻¹ productivity). This work demonstrates the power of biradical-mediated synergistic catalysis enabled by robust bicarbenium architecture and offers a general design strategy for next-generation, metal-free electrocatalysts, especially for redox transformations of open-shell substrates.
